The Northern red-backed vole (Myodes rutilus) exhibits a relatively rapid pace of life for a small arctic rodent. At a maternal body temperature maintained around 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females experience a gestation period lasting approximately 20 days [tg = approximately 20 days], a duration comparable to that documented in the closely related bank vole (Myodes glareolus). Newborn pups enter the world weighing just 2.9 grams [Wwb = 2.9 grams], an altricial state that necessitates intensive maternal care during the initial postnatal phase. This modest neonatal mass reflects the energetic constraints of a short boreal growing season, where rapid development is favored to prepare young for the onset of winter. The high metabolic costs of maintaining both pregnancy and lactation at cool ambient temperatures are partially offset by the vole's use of insulated nests beneath the snowpack.

Weaning represents a critical developmental transition for the offspring of this species. At the standard physiological temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], pups achieve nutritional independence from their mother approximately 20 days after birth [tx = approximately 20 days after birth]. This relatively early weaning age, again mirrored in the life-history data for Myodes glareolus, allows females to reduce the energetic burden of lactation and potentially initiate a subsequent litter within the same breeding season. Following weaning, the young voles enter a juvenile phase characterized by rapid somatic growth as they forage independently on berries, fungi, and arthropods. The timing of this dietary shift is crucial for accumulating sufficient body reserves before the protracted winter fast, and it typically coincides with peak summer resource availability in their tundra and taiga habitats.

Sexual maturation in female Northern red-backed voles occurs at a consistent interval following birth. Under normothermic conditions at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], the time from parturition to the onset of puberty is approximately 47 days following birth [tp = approximately 47 days following birth]. This developmental schedule, which again aligns with data reported for Myodes glareolus, enables females born early in the spring to achieve reproductive status and contribute to population recruitment within their first summer of life. Such rapid maturation is a hallmark of a species adapted to short, intense breeding windows in high-latitude environments. The attainment of sexual maturity is accompanied by morphological changes and the activation of ovarian cycles, at which point young females become capable of participating in the mating system that drives the species' characteristically high population turnover rates.

The ultimate adult body size attained by Northern red-backed voles is modest, reflecting their ecological position as a small herbivore within the arctic and subarctic food web. Field surveys and captive colony records indicate that asymptotic mass for healthy adults reaches approximately 29 grams [Wwi = approximately 29 grams]. Some populations exhibit a slightly larger terminal body size, with individuals occasionally recorded at 30 grams [Wwi = 30 grams], likely influenced by local variations in forage quality and habitat productivity. This relatively small body volume, combined with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, imposes substantial thermoregulatory costs in the boreal environment, requiring voles to maintain a high resting metabolic rate to sustain core temperature at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] during frigid winter conditions. Seasonally, adults may accumulate fat stores in autumn as a buffer against winter food scarcity.

Reproductive output in this species is structured to maximize recruitment during the brief summer pulse. Females typically produce litters of 3 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3 pups per litter], although litter size can vary with maternal condition and food abundance. The maximum annual reproductive rate, when calculated as the product of litter size and a high frequency of successive breeding events, has been estimated to be as high as 4.3 litters per year [F_R_i = 4.3 litters per year] under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. This potential for rapid, repeated breeding is balanced by a relatively short lifespan; the maximum documented longevity for the species, modeled after survival data for Myodes glareolus, is approximately 4.9 years [am = approximately 4.9 years] at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. High predation pressure from mustelids, raptors, and owls, coupled with severe winter mortality, ensures that few individuals attain this upper age limit in the wild.
